experiments.title: Q5 vs Q6: smaller, but not faster
experiments.summary: A Q5 file is about 10% smaller than Q6, so in theory the card has less to read per token and should write faster. On this card it was about 5% slower, because Intel's kernels for Q6_K are better optimised than Q5_K's. The only gain was 1.6 GB more free memory.

setup.engine: llama.cpp SYCL (July build), MTP draft n-max 2, 8-bit KV
setup.model: Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q6_K (22 GB) vs UD-Q5_K_M (19.9 GB)
setup.method: Same session, same Rune settings with only the model file changed; 400-token answer (short) and ~8K-token prompt (long), two runs each

experiments.verdict: Not adopted. Smaller isn't automatically faster: which formats the Intel kernels are tuned for matters more than file size. Q5 was deleted. (Q4_0 was faster in an earlier test because it's the best-tuned format of all, but it couldn't finish a hard task.)

experiments.title: Newer llama.cpp (b12716): faster benchmark, slower in real use
experiments.summary: I built the latest llama.cpp to replace my July build. The first build read prompts 2.3× slower because one build option, GGML_SYCL_F16, was missing. Rebuilt with it, llama-bench looked great. But in real use multi-token prediction (MTP) is broken on Intel in this version, and Rune fell to about 14 tok/s.

setup.engine: llama.cpp SYCL: July build (e9fa0781f) vs b12716 (bb692ef), both with GGML_SYCL_F16=ON
setup.model: Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q6_K, 8-bit KV, flash attention on
setup.method: llama-bench pp4096 / tg128 with the server stopped, then a test server with Rune's real settings, with and without MTP

charts.title: Real use: Rune's writing speed, short answer

experiments.verdict: Kept the July build live. b12716 without MTP would trade about a third of Rune's writing speed for 2× faster reading. With MTP it's slower at everything. It stays on disk for a re-test when a later release fixes MTP on Intel. Tip: if you build llama.cpp for Arc, check that GGML_SYCL_F16=ON is in your CMake cache.

experiments.title: Rune Deep: MTP at 192K, then a needle test
experiments.summary: Rune Deep used the same model with a 256K context but no MTP, so it was slow. MTP's draft memory grows with context, so it didn't fit at 256K or 224K, only at 192K. That made Deep about 80% faster. Then a needle test (a fact hidden two-thirds of the way through a huge document) crashed Deep twice. Plain Rune, with more free memory, passed it.

setup.model: Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q6_K: Deep at 192K + MTP vs Rune at 128K + MTP
setup.method: bench-rune.py (short answer + 8K prompt), then needle-test.py: one fact hidden at 66% of a generated auction ledger

charts.title: Needle test: tokens read before it finished or crashed
Deep's prompt reading slows with depth

experiments.verdict: Deep retired. Each crash followed the same chain: the attention routine ran out of working memory, fell back to a slower kernel, hit the driver's job timeout, and the GPU reset. Rune read 113K tokens in 872 s and found the fact, so long sessions stay on Rune. Free card memory, not the context number, decides how deep a model can go. Worth retrying with a future llama.cpp or a bigger card.

experiments.title: vLLM is back: clean starts after a firmware update
experiments.summary: vLLM was parked a week earlier because 3 of 14 cold starts hit a GPU fault while loading weights. Then I updated the host's firmware: BIOS 1.51, whose release notes include a Thunderbolt 4 power-negotiation fix, plus the CPU microcode and Intel ME updates that came with it. With the same kernel, compute runtime and vLLM image, it started cleanly every time. I can't prove which part of the update fixed it. It's now a second model in llama-swap, called Rune Fast.

setup.engine: vLLM 0.27.2rc1 XPU (Docker) vs llama.cpp SYCL, both behind llama-swap
setup.model: Qwen3.8-27B GPTQ Int4 + MTP4 vs UD-Q6_K + MTP2
setup.method: 10 back-to-back cold starts counting kernel engine resets, then 5 rounds of Rune → vLLM → Rune swaps with a 400-token coding answer (thinking off), timed by wall clock

charts.title: Clean vLLM cold starts
charts.unit: % of starts with no GPU fault

charts.title: Time to swap the model in

experiments.verdict: Adopted as an option, not the default. Rune Fast runs at 59–62 tok/s with 0 engine resets in 15 starts, but it takes ~165 s to swap in and is text-only for now. I pick it for long coding sessions in Continue and Qwen Code, then switch back so the phone app gets Rune quickly. Still to test: long contexts, thinking on, and pictures.

experiments.title: 8-bit KV cache + moving vision onto the B70
experiments.summary: Quantizing the KV cache to 8-bit freed about 3.6 GB of VRAM, which made room to run the vision projector on the GPU instead of the CPU. Writing speed barely moved; prompt reading dropped about 23%, and reading pictures got about 5× faster.

setup.method: Custom Python bench: 400-token coding answer (short), ~8,100-token prompt (long), timestamp in every prompt to defeat the prompt cache

experiments.verdict: Kept both. An 8K prompt now takes ~12.6 s to read instead of ~9.7 s, but pictures are ~5× faster and there's ~2.9 GB of headroom. A third MTP draft token fit with the extra memory but was no faster on short answers and slower on long ones (27.4 vs 28.5 tok/s), so it stayed at 2.

experiments.title: vLLM (4-bit + MTP) vs llama.cpp (Q6 + MTP)
experiments.summary: A community recipe runs Qwen3.8-27B on the B70 with vLLM's XPU image, a GPTQ 4-bit model and 4-token MTP. It nearly doubled writing speed on the same coding prompt.

setup.model: Qwen3.8-27B GPTQ Int4 + MTP vs UD-Q6_K + MTP
setup.method: Same coding question in both; vLLM limited to one request at a time

experiments.verdict: Parked, not adopted. 3 of 14 cold starts hit a GPU fault while copying weights (xe engine reset) and vLLM hung instead of exiting. Start-up also takes 130–200 s vs ~25 s for llama.cpp. Re-test bar: 0 failures in 5 starts. (Update: it passed after a host firmware update on Nov 22, see the top of this page.)

experiments.title: Q4 vs Q6 quantization: speed vs finishing the job
experiments.summary: A 4-bit file would free 4–6 GB of VRAM, so I tested two 4-bit quants against Q6. On this backend Q4_K_XL was actually slower than Q6, while Q4_0 was much faster, because llama.cpp's SYCL kernels are best tuned for Q4_0 and Q6_K.

setup.method: Same coding prompt; quality test = Pratt-parser calculator with pytest tests

experiments.verdict: Stayed on Q6. Q4_0 never delivered an answer to the hard prompt: twice it thought for ~32,000 tokens (850 s) and was cut off, with its reasoning degrading into loops. Q6 finished with 71/71 of its own tests passing and 0 mismatches against Python on 5,000 random expressions.

experiments.title: Multi-token prediction (MTP): 40–60% faster writing
experiments.summary: Qwen3.8 GGUFs include a small MTP head that drafts the next tokens; the main model verifies them, so accepted guesses are nearly free. It only speeds up writing, not prompt reading. No rebuild or extra download was needed.

setup.method: Same coding prompt, with and without MTP

experiments.verdict: Adopted. 78% of drafted tokens were accepted with thinking off, 58% with thinking on. n-max 3 didn't fit in VRAM at the time (out-of-device-memory at load). Tool calling still worked.

experiments.title: Flash attention × micro-batch size
experiments.summary: The old default (flash attention off, ubatch 512) was picked because flash attention was slower at small micro-batches. At ubatch 2048 it wins, and it also cut VRAM use by ~2.2 GB.

setup.method: llama-bench -p 4096 -n 64 -b 2048 -r 2, with the server and watchdog stopped

experiments.verdict: Adopted -fa 1 --ubatch-size 2048. In real use (7.7K-token prompt at 64K context) prompt reading went from ~600 to ~880–900 tok/s (+50%), generation at that depth from 17.5 to 18.55 tok/s, and free VRAM from 4.0 to 6.3 GB.

experiments.title: The 10× fix: making sure work runs on the B70 at all
experiments.summary: The host has two Intel GPUs: the B70 and the Meteor Lake iGPU. Without Level Zero dev headers at build time, SYCL only saw the iGPU, and without pinning, work could land there. Everything "worked", just painfully slowly.

setup.engine: llama.cpp SYCL, rebuilt with libze-dev; --main-gpu 0 -sm none
setup.method: Generation speed before and after pinning to the B70

experiments.verdict: Lesson: "active (running)" doesn't mean it's on the right GPU. Check that cmake reports Level Zero found, pin the device, and verify with lspci and --list-devices after every cold boot.
